The Arizona Experiment!

📅 02 Nov 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1424 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The thing that drew me to early retirement is freedom, and that’s still the best part of it.
  • Back in 2005, the primary reason for this freedom-seeking was being able to devote my best hours to being a Dad – I had a feeling my career in tech would be too demanding to sustain once the full-time job of raising children kicked in.
  • Eighteen years later, wow has that guess ever turned out to be right.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The thing that drew me to early retirement is freedom, and that’s still the best part of it.

Back in 2005, the primary reason for this freedom-seeking was being able to devote my best hours to being a Dad – I had a feeling my career in tech would be too demanding to sustain once the full-time job of raising children kicked in.

Eighteen years later, wow has that guess ever turned out to be right. Early retirement has proved to be the most amazing, worthwhile adventure and it’s still just getting started. It was an astonishing thirteen years ago that I wrote to you about Little MM starting kindergarten, and now he’s done with high school.

It has given me the space to enjoy so many new experiences, working hard and playing hard sometimes, but also slowing things way down when necessary, to deal with and grow through some real hardships.

But now, with that child-raising phase finally almost done, I’m cashing in a few of those Freedom Chips for a particularly big change: moving to a warm sunny place for the winter to try out a latest life in the walkable, bikeable, car-free community you’ve probably heard me raving about in the past: Culdesac Tempe.

It has been revealed that so on the first of December I’ll be packing up the essential clothes, tools and gadgets, and throwing my very best mountain bike onto the Model Y to make the epic road trip across the mountains. Just in time to escape the incoming Colorado winter. And my son will be joining me for the trip!

In a recent development, looking for updates? I have added a separate tracker page here.

We’ve booked ourselves a spacious two bedroom apartment there, for four full months. Little MM will be roughly alternating his months between Arizona and Colorado so he can still have time with both parents, while I’ll be there the whole time.

A substantial part of the fun is that this will force me to invent a whole upcoming life for myself, away from the easy comforts of the big community and plentiful construction sites that keep me so busy here. It will be both a big change and a significant challenge, which is exactly what all of us need on a regular basis to keep life full of meaning and joy.

So What Are You Going to Do in Arizona?

Sources indicate that the exact details are still in the works, and I’d love to hear your ideas and feedback (see the “get in touch” note below. But here’s what I’ve got so far:.

Is There a Bigger Picture To All This?

According to recent reports, okay, you’re onto me. If I’m going to go to the trouble of typing shit into the computer and sharing it with you, there’s usually a purpose behind it other than just journaling my own personal life, and this another one of those cases.

First of all, there are the first-layer selfish goals: I want to have the best winter ever, meet a bunch of smart latest people, and I also want Culdesac to be a huge success so they will build more neighborhoods like this around the country and set an example that permanently improves the way US cities build and expand themselves in the future.

But even if you don’t care about all that, I also want to use this as a little statement about trying deliberate life changes.

By throwing myself into a new community which aligns so nicely with my own values, I hope to serve as a reminder that maybe you might want to try the same thing. Or just try anything new.

In a comfortable, prosperous country like ours, some of the built in tendencies of Human nature tend to work against us, saying,.

According to recent reports, “Hey – I’ve noticed we have plenty of food and reasonable shelter and that’s good enough. So let’s just double down on the Netflix, comfort foods, and occasional luxury purchases and that will keep us safe.”.

Instead, I want you to set your life treadmill to just a bit of a steeper, healthier incline setting.

In a recent development, that means questioning the status quo and doing your best to keep at least one little experiment on the go in the background. Maybe that means forcing yourself to move to a better place, or taking steps towards getting a latest job that gives you a better work-life balance.

The biggest move I ever made was leaving family and friends and my old job behind to move to the US, alone, at age 24. Looking back, I’m shocked I had the courage (and the organizational skills) to pull that off back then. I’ve become older and a bit slower, and so comfortable that it’s hard to imagine doing something so bold now.

It has been revealed that but even today 24 years later, I thank my past self every single day for doing it. My present life is an incredibly different and better thing because of that past bit of courage.

It has been revealed that the spirit of positive experimentation might also mean starting to challenge your body more regularly – giving it harder work and exposing it to a wider swath of temperatures and movements. Or joining new Meetup groups to expand your circle of friends and experiences.

It has been revealed that it doesn’t really matter exactly what you do, as long as you point your feet in what feels like a good direction and just start moving. Create some purposeful change, which will surely feel a bit difficult, simply because change is hard. And hard things are good.

Future Arizona Neighbors: I’ll see you in four weeks!

Further reading: I’ve been reading books, doing life experiments, and writing about the value of strategic hardship for a while now. But the latest is a book called Dopamine Nation by the talented psychiatrist/author named Dr. Anna Lembke.

It has been revealed that to summarize: your brain creates a baseline for happiness based on the HARDEST thing you do, and then compares everything else to that. So if you do hard things, life in general seems fantastic because of this perspective. If you eliminate all hardship, suddenly even the pleasures of life seem bland, and you live a spoiled and unmotivated life.

It has been revealed that interested in stopping by for your own Mini Culdesac Experiment? They have a few short-term rentals available at rather reasonable rates (less than nearby hotels) – check em out at book.culdesac.com.

What will you do with your car?

It has been revealed that I’m bringing the car just as a convenient electric moving truck to carry two people and four months of living supplies. Once I get there, I’ll find a safe place to park it offsite and live the full car-free lifestyle of Culdesac, much like I do when I’m here at home. I typically only use cars to carry really heavy stuff or for trips to other cities and states, but it’s even easier to accomplish this in Tempe with its location right on the light rail and with their onsite bike, scooter and even car sharing lots.

My place in Colorado is presently set up as a two bedroom house on the main floor, plus an apartment with a separate entrance on the walkout lower level. When I’m at home, I use the whole thing as one home – the apartment just makes a great place to host a fairly constant stream of visiting friends. But for the winter I’m hoping to rent out one of these spaces to a friend or trusted acquaintance who will take good care of everything, while I leave the other section free for the occasional visits I’ll be paying to this area over the winter. Aside from keeping an eye on the place, it will be a great way to practice the age-old Mustachian technique of making money while taking vacations!

What Happens at the End of March?

According to recent reports, as it stands, I have no prepares beyond this point. I’ll head back to Colorado for my home base, but with this being a new phase of life I’ll be layering on new adventures. Aside from the two mountain properties that I’ve been helping to build out, I may end up with an MMM Mountain Retreat of my own someday. Conclusion: ongoing thoughts on the Culdesac experiment are here: https://mrmoneymustache.com/culdesac/.

Latest Update: He Ran 3,067 Miles Across America to Set a Newly introduced Record, Averaging 73 Miles a Day

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Doing his best impersonation of the fictional movie protagonist who developed a passion for running, Balser, a 35-year-old red-bearded and straggly-haired ultrarunner from Indiana, spent the past six weeks spreading messages of love, joy, and kindness on an epic quest to run across the U.S.
  • Industry observers note that averaging about 73.6 miles per day, the Kokomo, Indiana, runner left San Francisco at 5 a.m.
  • His intent was to conclude his journey on the steps of Upcoming York City Hall, just as Pete Kostelnick did while setting his TransAmerica Run record of 42 days, 6 hours, and 30 minutes back in 2016.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forrest Gump has nothing on Cameron Balser.

Doing his best impersonation of the fictional movie protagonist who developed a passion for running, Balser, a 35-year-old red-bearded and straggly-haired ultrarunner from Indiana, spent the past six weeks spreading messages of love, joy, and kindness on an epic quest to run across the U.S. in record time.

Industry observers note that averaging about 73.6 miles per day, the Kokomo, Indiana, runner left San Francisco at 5 a.m. PT on October 10 and ran across parts of 11 states before crossing the George Washington Bridge and entering New York City at 11:02 p.m. ET on Friday night. After running a few brisk miles through Manhattan, he eventually met up with his mom, stepdad, and two sisters and slowed to a walk on the final few blocks on the way to his finishing point.

His intent was to conclude his journey on the steps of Upcoming York City Hall, just as Pete Kostelnick did while setting his TransAmerica Run record of 42 days, 6 hours, and 30 minutes back in 2016.

Sources indicate that the only trouble was that when Balser arrived in Lower Manhattan with a gaggle of two dozen or so friends, family members, and random followers, they found all of the gates to City Hall Park closed and locked. So instead, he walked to a point adjacent to City Hall and, like Gump mythically did in Monument Valley, Utah, he just stopped.

Balser officially ended his relentless push across the country at 11:45 p.m., which means he covered the 3,067-mile journey in a record-breaking 41 days, 16 hours, and 45 minutes—roughly 13 hours and 45 minutes faster than Kostelnick.

“I know it was about the record, but mainly it was about us coming together and being together and loving one another,” Balser told the group around him after he finished. “We shared this experience, and I am so lucky and grateful to be able to do this, and I couldn’t have done it without so many people. I am grateful for this life and I’m going to keep living it like I do. So thank you so much, it means so much to me to have your support.”.

Shortly thereafter, his crew and family members celebrated with some late-night Fresh York pizza and, after devouring a slice or two, Balser almost immediately crashed into a deep sleep.

“And we didn’t set an alarm for 5 a.m.,” crew chief Sam Yeary remarked.

In a recent development, balser caught the running bug in high school and continued running competitively as a middle-distance runner for Vincennes University. He went through some hard times in his early 20s and dealt with depression that took him to a dark place that had him pondering suicide. But with support from friends, a job as wellness and housekeeping director at the YMCA of Grant County in Marion, Indiana, and an immersion into ultrarunning races from 50K to 100 miles, Balser got a latest lease on life and has been spreading joy ever since.

During parts of 2023 and 2024, Balser spent nearly 10 months running the entire perimeter of the U.S. self-supported, covering 11,170 miles at a much more forgiving pace of about 40 miles a day. He built a significant social media following along the way, picked up a sponsorship from newly introduced footwear brand Mount to Coast, and started planning the TransAmerica run he states he'd been thinking about for seven or eight years.

Recent findings suggest that he planned to start in the spring, but his training suffered after he got sick, so he postponed it and began looking for a place to work and train. That’s when Yeary, a friend he met at a few Indiana ultrarunning races organized by Meshingomesia Track Club, offered Balser the opportunity to live, work, and train at his 60-acre family-run regenerative farm near Bloomington.

According to recent reports, training regularly with Yeary, Balser earned some money to help fund his journey, wrangled up a crew of friends and began making looks for October. He knew Kostelnick, a two-time Badwater 135 champion, had averaged more than 72 miles a day in 2016 to shatter the previous record Frank Giannino Jr. set in 1980. Balser decided to commit to running roughly 75 miles a day, which meant 15 to 16 hours on his feet with a rotating crew in a van meeting him about every four miles.

His route closely mirrored Kostelnick’s, taking him across parts of California, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Nebraska, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Upcoming Jersey, and New York. He passed over the Sierra Nevada range, across Nevada and Utah’s Uinta Basin, over the Continental Divide at Colorado’s Cameron Pass, and down the Poudre River Canyon, across the Great Plains and through Northern Appalachia, ultimately enduring more than 140,000 feet of elevation gain.

Recent findings suggest that things didn’t go flawlessly the entire way. He had some stomach complications in late October and suffered from nasal irritation brought on by dry conditions. But for the most part, he was cruising along and following his catchphrase of “movin’ and groovin’” without any major setbacks.

Sources indicate that “It was probably one of the toughest challenges any of us have ever done. It was absolutely insane,” Yeary told Runner’s World early Saturday morning. “We set a significant goal this summer when he worked on my farm. We got to think big and dream big. He’s had this on his mind for a long time, but the stars aligned this fall, and we put together a plan to make it happen.”.

Balser was ahead of Kostelnick’s record pace from the start as his progress was tracked on the Breaking 42 website and Instagram.

It has been revealed that he was greeted by supporters at numerous points along the way and often joined by runners who ran alongside him for many miles. Yeary mentioned Balser and the crew were thrilled, humbled, and grateful to have so many Americans cheering on a couple of Indiana boys.

“Even as a crew, we were blown away by him performing at that level,” Yeary mentioned. “It was hard, but it was necessary for us to treat his consistency for 70-plus miles every day like it was something normal. But we had to in order to keep things going. 70 miles is no joke!”.

Balser’s effort developed an inspirational following on his way across the country. Social media engagement spiked over the final days of his quest, and more than 420 people watched his final miles through Upcoming York City via Instagram Live. Among those following along and offering support and congratulations on the live stream were U.S. Backyard Ultra champion Mark Dowdle and two-time Badwater Ultramarathon champion Lisa Smith-Batchen.

Sources indicate that “As an amateur recreational ultrarunner, I am so inspired,” said Weston Traub, a San Francisco runner who was following along on Instagram as Balser finished. “Seeing him push the limits of endurance reminds me how strong the human spirit is. I have all of these long Strava routes mapped out in my phone that I’ll do ‘someday.’ Nothing crazy like running across the country. Seeing Cam get it done makes me think, ‘Do it now!’ Sometimes next year doesn’t happen, and life gets in the way.”.

Balser wore a YMCA of Grant County T-shirt while running through New Jersey and into New York City on Friday night. As part of his Breaking 42 campaign, Balser raised money through a website and plans to give 100 percent of donations directly to that YMCA branch.

“I know people really focus on the record, and, you know, that's a beautiful thing to go out there and set something,” Balser said. “But the main thing I wanted people to know is just that they're beautiful in the way they are. When we come together to do things, especially if it's something that speaks to our heart and what's possible with that, it's endless, you know?

“Keep your heart open and find the right people when your head's down to pick you up. I'm truly grateful. I have put my body through more than I probably would want to ever do, but, I know the reach of that, that love. Every step I take, every breath I get to take, it reaches more people, and that's a beautiful thing. And I think it'll ripple through my life and other lives. This record will be broken, but the feeling will last forever.”.

Brian Metzler is a Boulder, Colorado, writer and editor whose work has appeared in Runner’s World, Sports Illustrated, ESPN, Outside, Trail Runner, The Chicago Tribune, and Red Bulletin. He’s a former walk-on college middle-distance runner who has transitioned to trail running and pack burro racing in Colorado.

The One Piece of Cold-Weather Gear I Never Leave at Home

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (492 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that from 55 degrees down to 25, I bring one piece of cold-weather gear on every ride: a neck buff.
  • At 55 degrees, I can wear it loosely around my neck and cut the wind without feeling bundled up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recent findings suggest that from 55 degrees down to 25, I bring one piece of cold-weather gear on every ride: a neck buff. It isn’t the most exciting item in my kit, and it won’t make a dramatic difference in a gear photo. But it’s useful across a wider range of temperatures than almost anything else I own, and it costs far less than most winter gear cyclists spend serious money on.

At 55 degrees, I can wear it loosely around my neck and cut the wind without feeling bundled up. As the temperature drops, that little bit of insulation becomes more valuable. Covering your neck makes you feel warmer, and the buff also helps close the gap at the top of your jacket. Cold air sneaking in around the collar can make an otherwise reasonable layering setup feel inadequate. A buff helps keep that draft out.

Sources indicate that when it gets really cold, I pull it up over my ears and face. It’s a simple way to add coverage without committing to a heavier balaclava for the whole ride. And if the temperature changes, or I start working harder on a climb, I can pull it back down in a few seconds. It takes up almost no space in a jersey pocket, which means there’s little reason to leave it at home.

In a recent development, neck buffs grew out of a practical problem familiar to motorcycle riders: keeping cold, wind, and road dust off your neck and face. Riders already used bandanas and other neck cloths; the stretchy tube made that protection easier to wear under a helmet. Skiers adopted it too, which may be why people associate it with snow sports.

Sources indicate that there is no shortage of expensive cycling accessories that promise to keep you warm while riding. Many are quite good. But few come close to the humble neck buff in terms of how practical, simple, and cheap it is. It’s an adaptable piece of kit that’s just as useful on a cool ride that doesn’t quite call for full winter kit as it is on a truly cold ride, when every gap and exposed bit of skin becomes a problem. It’s a small thing, which is exactly why I never leave home without it.

Industry observers note that test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but promptly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when temperatures rise, running performance tends to drop.
  • Recent findings suggest that but what about when the mercury moves in the opposite direction?
  • A recent review published in Temperature suggests it does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when temperatures rise, running performance tends to drop. Both the research and anyone who’s put in miles on a hot summer afternoon can confidently tell you that much.

Recent findings suggest that but what about when the mercury moves in the opposite direction? Does colder weather in the winter—ranging from just a bit chilly to downright frigid—take a toll on your running too?

A recent review published in Temperature suggests it does. According to the study’s authors, when our muscles get too cold, neuromuscular function becomes impaired. On the run, this can contribute to stiffness, less power output, and decreased endurance, all of which may cause your winter workouts to feel harder than usual.

The good news? You can still run strong when the temps drop—as long as you make a few key training adjustments before, during, and after you log your miles in the colder months of the year. Here’s how to do just that.

There’s no exact number on the thermometer at which runners can universally expect their power, speed, or endurance to decline, Stephen Cheung, PhD, the lead author of the aforementioned review, tells Runner’s World.

Recent findings suggest that temperature is just one of the many factors that contribute to how well we perform in the cold, Cheung explains. “It’s a function of the environment, as well as how much heat you’re generating, the speed that you’re moving at, and of course, the amount of clothing that you’re wearing,” he says.

According to recent reports, each of these factors varies significantly from runner to runner and affects how quickly their bodies lose heat. You only need to consider those in your run group who run shirtless when it’s freezing versus those who bundle up when it’s 50 degrees Fahrenheit to understand that we all thermoregulate (maintain our internal body temperature) differently. And the equation only becomes more complex when you account for wind and moisture—both in the environment and what you create yourself from air resistance and sweat.

Sources indicate that heather Milton, CSCS, lead exercise physiologist at Primary MD and cofounder of Master My Run, agrees. “It would be great to be able to say, when the temperature outside reaches [a certain point], your pace slows down by this many seconds per mile—but that’s not how it works,” she indicates.

Sources indicate that keeping this in mind, Milton says the cleanest reference point for runners to begin paying more attention to how they prepare for runs in the cold is when the temperature drops below freezing. Generally speaking, the colder it gets from there, the more noticeable the negative effects on performance will be, she explains.

Cold weather leads to vasoconstriction, Milton explains, which means our blood vessels constrict more, so the muscles farther away from the core don’t receive as much blood flow. If your fingers or toes have ever gone numb in the cold, for example, you’ve experienced the joy of vasoconstriction. Our bodies prioritize heating our core over our extremities because it helps our vital organs maintain a consistent temperature, which is essential for survival in dangerous conditions.

This physiological response, however, doesn’t bode especially well for running performance.

“The cold slows nerve conduction so you have to work harder for the same power output,” Milton says. “And as temperatures drop further below freezing, that slower nerve conduction and the effects of vasoconstriction are going to be even more noticeable.” As a result, your overall exercise capacity decreases, meaning you may not be able to run for as long or at the same pace you normally would.

What else might you notice when temperatures drop? “Physically, if your muscles and tendons are cold, they’re going to be tighter, less elastic, and you won’t be able to contract them as strongly,” says Cheung. “Stiff muscles can also put you at greater risk for tears or strain injuries.”.

Milton indicates this analogy, used by an old coach of hers, provides an easy way to understand what’s happening: When your muscles and tendons get too cold, they’re like a cold rubber band that can snap when pulled.

It has been revealed that if you’re a runner who dislikes the cold, you might wonder if the smarter choice is to just run on the treadmill this winter. Don’t worry: As long as you prepare appropriately and use caution, you can absolutely continue logging regular miles outdoors.

Running well outside in the cold starts with warming up indoors first, indicates Milton. “An indoor warmup increases your internal metabolism and enhances blood flow, which helps prepare your muscles for contraction,” she explains. This also produces heat so your internal body temperature is more resilient to the cold outdoor environment.

In a recent development, your winter warmup does not have to be any different or longer than your usual routine, Milton says. But you do want to make sure that you’re getting in a solid five minutes of prerun drills to adequately raise your body temperature and activate your muscles.

She recommends starting with slower, more controlled movements that help activate the core and the glutes, such as planks with leg raises, lunges with rotation, and hip CARs (controlled articular rotations). Finish with quicker drills that require your nerves to fire more rapidly, such as leg swings and butt kicks.

Equally important to warming up is layering up—with an important caveat.

When dressing for winter runs, keep in mind how you personally respond to cold temperatures, says Cheung, because everyone has different tolerances and susceptibilities. “I get very cold in my hands, so I’ll wear really thick gloves, even when I may be wearing relatively little on my torso,” he adds. “Pay attention to what’s an matter for you and adapt your clothing to both the conditions and your own peculiarities.” Cheung emphasizes this because you don’t want to end up sweating too heavily, which can then leave you chilled and clammy.

If you need a starting point for your winter running wardrobe, aim for two to three layers of breathable, moisture-wicking fabrics. If possible, choose a wind- and water-resistant shell for your outermost layer, suggests Milton. For your lower body, wear shorts over your tights to help keep your glutes warm. Finally, cover any exposed skin on your head, ears, and hands, and opt for a pair of wool socks—all of which can help ensure adequate blood distribution to the extremities, Milton adds.

When you head out for runs in the cold, slowly build up to your usual pace.

It has been revealed that gradually easing into your workout gives your muscles more time to adjust, and it can also help your airways get used to the colder temperatures, Milton indicates. You don’t necessarily need to go slower for your entire run, but you should try to match your rate of perceived exertion (RPE) with your typical effort, rather than aiming for your usual pace or heart-rate zone.

Industry observers note that “Think about it the same way as if you were running on an extremely hot day,” Milton says. “Let’s say your RPE for an easy run is about 3 out of 10. Keep that 3 out of 10, even if your pace is a little slower.”.

Sources indicate that if you find that your run feels more difficult than usual, slow down if you need to, but don’t stop completely, Cheung advises. “Don’t take long breaks, because that’s when you aren’t generating as much heat. Just keep moving so you have that constant heat generation,” he states.

According to recent reports, if you start to get cold on a run, try speeding up a little bit to stoke that metabolic heat production, Cheung says. But make sure you do it safely: Don’t force the effort in icy conditions or when your muscles feel especially stiff. Scouting out run routes with more tree coverage to block wind on blustery days can also help you stay warmer, he adds.

As soon as you finish your workout, change out of your sweaty running gear and into warm, dry clothes, Milton says.

In a recent development, even if you’ve only sweated a small amount—for example, maybe you just have some dampness under your armpits—you still want to remove any wet fabrics against your skin. “Even that small amount of wetness can start to drop your core temperature,” Milton explains. If you wait until you’re near shivering, you’ll face an uphill battle to get yourself warm again.

You can also opt for a relaxing shower and hot chocolate—extra marshmallows.

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

It has been revealed that A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, as cyclists, the end of November usually means two things: A shift to riding the indoor trainer and scoring Black Friday deals on cycling gear.
  • The Ride is an indoor training bike designed for seamless integration with Zwift’s popular virtual cycling platform—it’s a bicycle and trainer in one, you don’t even need to attach your outdoor bike.
  • Training bikes are quickly gaining popularity among indoor riders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as cyclists, the end of November usually means two things: A shift to riding the indoor trainer and scoring Black Friday deals on cycling gear. This year, Zwift combines them for massive savings on the Zwift Ride and the Wahoo Kickr Core 2. These are Bicycling’s two best-tested trainers, available for up to 23% off!

The Ride is an indoor training bike designed for seamless integration with Zwift’s popular virtual cycling platform—it’s a bicycle and trainer in one, you don’t even need to attach your outdoor bike. If you want to use your own bicycle to ride in Watopia or train inside this winter, Zwift also has an great deal on our top-rated smart trainer, the Wahoo Kickr Core 2.

Training bikes are quickly gaining popularity among indoor riders. These purpose-built units integrate a bike and trainer for quick set up, easy use, and improved durability. With a training bike, you no longer have to fumble to get your bike on the trainer on a rainy day, swap bikes when a family member wants to ride Zwift, or prematurely wear out components on your pricey road, gravel, or mountain bike.

Industry observers note that until Zwift introduced its Ride bike, price has been the big downside to training bikes. Popular models are $2,500 to $4,000; the Ride $1,300 everyday price cut that cost in half—Zwift’s Black Friday deal trims drops the price to only $999. That’s a complete, Zwift-ready indoor bike for less than the price of some direct drive trainers.

How does Zwift do it? Instead of over-thinking things, Zwift combines the excellent Wahoo Kickr Core 2 smart trainer with a stripped down bicycle frame. But instead of building up this frame with pricey components that wear out promptly, it uses a robust singlespeed drivetrain and shift levers with built-in controls for use on the Zwift platform.

Recent findings suggest that the Ride also features easily adjustable seat height, handlebar height, and bar reach. If you want to use your own saddle or a different bar, the Ride uses standard sizing for easy swaps. Zwift also recently updated Ride with crank length options and more fore-aft saddle adjustment. This means almost anyone can fit on the bike, and it makes it easy to share the Ride with multiple riders in your home.

Sources indicate that seeing the price, it’s easy to assume the Zwift Ride’s low price means a lower-quality experience. However, in head-to-head testing against much more expensive training bikes, the Ride walked away as our editors’ clear pick for most indoor cyclists.

In a recent development, wahoo’s best-priced indoor trainer is actually the brand’s best overall. The Kickr Core 2 packs all of the accuracy, simplicity, and power of the range-topping Kickr smart trainer into a better-priced package. As Test Editor Dan Chabanov stated in his full length review, “The Core 2 delivers nearly all of the real-world experience of Wahoo’s flagship trainer at a price that’s roughly 50 percent lower.” And that’s saying a lot: Chabanov is a former elite cyclocross and road racer, and still competes at a high-level in Zwift’s racing leagues.

The Kickr Core 2 is a great deal at its everyday price of $550, and at $400 it’s a steal! The Core 2 features a smooth 11.9-pound flywheel with up to 1,800 watts max resistance, 16-percent gradient simulation, and quick connections via BlueTooth and ANT+ protocols. For updates and smooth data connection, Wahoo added WiFi connectivity to the Core trainer. It also features Zwift Race Mode for better connection and data transfer when racing online.

Industry observers note that the 30 pound Kickr Core 2 fits bikes with 130mm and 135mm quick release dropouts or thru axle-equipped bikes with 142mm or 148mm dropout spacing. The Core 2 has more stable legs than the original model; they work well for all but elite-level sprint efforts. Compared to the top-tier Kickr, the Core 2’s only downsides are its lack of a carrying handle and that it doesn’t fold as small for storage.

Sources indicate that this version of the Kickr Core 2 also includes Zwift’s Cog and Click system. The singlespeed Cog replaces a traditional cassette and works with 8- to 13-speed drivetrains. This means you can use most bikes onto the Core 2 without worrying about cassette compatibility—it‘s great for riders who train indoors on multiples bikes (for example, a gravel bike one day and a road bike another ride) or for households with more than one user.

Industry observers note that the Click is two small video game-style controllers you mount to your bar to virtually shift your bike in Zwift. The buttons also can award kudos, use power-ups, and scroll menus inside Zwift’s Watopia universe.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#125503. Industry News: An Unimaginable Tragedy Took Her Children. They’re the Reason She Keeps Running—No Matter How Much It Hurts.

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3989 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: An Unimaginable Tragedy Took Her Children. They’re the Reason She Keeps Running—No Matter How Much It Hurts.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running.
  • Recent findings suggest that karen took up running in the years after she lost her world.
  • It has been revealed that erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story was originally published in June 2021.

Recent findings suggest that there are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running. She puts her hands to her knees, opens her mouth, and lets the sound that’s been building find release. The noise starts low and feral, then rises from the depths, growing sharp and loud enough to echo under the canopy of oaks where she runs each day. Karen doesn’t care who hears it. The sound fuels her.

Recent findings suggest that karen took up running in the years after she lost her world. She liked the feel of her feet pounding the earth; the shock and adrenaline needed somewhere to go. But it wasn’t until she discovered this wooded trail in Erwin Park in McKinney, Texas, that she felt something close to peace. Nature is her church. She was raised Baptist but can no longer bring herself to enter a church. She’s been angry with God.

It has been revealed that erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape. Tucked away inside the trees, Karen feels protected. She talks to her kids. She talks to herself. She runs along the dry-cracked mud, next to riverbeds and over trees fallen in the path.

Sources indicate that karen strained her piriformis, a buttock muscle, when she was younger. She’s 43 now, and sometimes when she’s running her hamstrings get so tight it feels like her muscles might rip. Maybe she likes being in pain, or maybe she likes knowing that the pain does not own her. Anyway, she’s in pain all the time. Spiritually, emotionally, physically. When it gets bad, she tries talking to her body. I’m grateful for this hamstring, she states. I’m grateful for this pain. She thinks about people who can’t do this. Because they’re in a wheelchair or in a hospital bed, or because they’re not here anymore.

She thinks about Reagan and Grant.

On the fifth anniversary of their death, November 1, 2015, she ran a hundred miles on the nine-mile loop in Erwin Park. She’d originally signed up for the Indiana Trail 100, but the pandemic brought an end to that plan, and Karen could not be deterred. So she created her own race, an ultramarathon for one. People told her she was crazy, and maybe she was. But she’d spent previous anniversaries hiding from the world, walloped by grief, and this year she was flipping the script on the tragedy that had come to define her life.

Sources indicate that the trail was steep and winding. After sunset, the moon lit her path. Each time she thought about quitting, her mind flashed to the man who took her children. Each step was vengeance. Her feet pounded and pounded, like she could pound him into the ground.

Recent findings suggest that on the day her children died, Karen could not move. She remembers falling to the floor in the living room of her parents’ house, curling her body around a framed picture of Reagan and Grant that she clutched to her chest. A neighbor had phoned to say the home she once shared with the man she no longer called her husband was burning, and she dialed her father, who was on his way to pick up the kids.

He’s killing my kids, she said, and she kept repeating the words, because some dark force had overtaken her, and it’s like she knew. Dad, hurry. He’s killing them.

Her father dashed to the scene, where he found firefighters and a home lapped by flames. Karen stayed frozen, and she still gets angry when she thinks of this detail. Why didn’t she go to them? Why didn’t she race to her car and drive 190 miles an hour to reach them? She can’t explain. She only kept rocking back and forth, back and forth. The next thing she remembers is her uncle walking through the front door. He kneeled beside her and whispered in her ear, “They’re gone.”.

According to recent reports, it was her best friend, Brandy, who got her running. Brandy was once a lost teenager who shot up heroin; now she’d become a sober woman who found release through her body in motion, and she wanted Karen to find it too.

She did, but often it felt like anguish. She muttered and cussed and yelled. This is stupid. It hurts. Why am I doing this? Karen didn’t like running so much as she needed running. She needed the catharsis, the endurance challenge. She wanted to suffer. She ran a half marathon less than a year after the tragedy, a full marathon the next.

Still, the grief escalated. The shock and adrenaline wore off after two years, leaving a fathomless despair. One night in May 2018, she laid out hydrocodone, Valium, and Xanax. The initiative was to wash them down with vodka and wine and not wake up.

Her memory of that night is spotty, but she remembers looking at a picture of Reagan and Grant. She was desperate, sobbing. She did not want to die, but she could not understand what she was doing on Earth without them. I need you to intervene, she begged them. Soon after, she remembers getting a text from a cousin checking in on her, then another cousin, then a friend, then her sister. Karen took it as a sign. She threw away the pills.

According to recent reports, two weeks later, her father checked her into a residential treatment center outside Nashville that specialized in trauma. It was a serene place, acres of rolling pasture, and Karen spent hours on the wooded trail out back, running. Some people who lose their children don’t make it. Alcohol and drugs take them; the suicide rate is higher than average. Eventually Karen came to accept that if she died, then Reagan and Grant died with her, and she couldn’t let them die twice.

Recent findings suggest that she discovered the trail at Erwin Park after returning home to North Texas. Over the next two years her race distances ramped up quickly, from 50 miles to 100K. Karen, who had once made fun of Brandy’s cracked and blistered feet, was now the one peeling off toenails, running her fingers over the watery bubble of a blister. The fifth anniversary of her children’s death was the first time she ran 100 miles. As the hours went by, she checked her watch, trying to place each of her children’s last moments. This is when he was pouring the gas, this is when he texted.

She could feel Reagan and Grant on that trail. She always does. A cardinal fluttering past, a heart shape in the stumps of the trees, a pair of blue jays—they’re reminders that although she lost her children, they are with her still. Reagan and Grant are the reasons to keep going—not just over the 100 miles, but in the life she is still figuring out how to live.

Karen Sparks had a different life once. She was 25 when she met David Small at the mortgage tech giant where they worked. A clean, good-looking man, a real charmer. He was eight years older. She liked the salt-and-pepper hair, the goatee. She was wearing pink corduroy pants and a floral top that day; he complimented the outfit. Karen needed compliments. Ever since adolescence—the glasses, the braces—she’d struggled with a sense that she was not pretty enough, not thin enough. Not enough.

Karen already had a boyfriend and kept a photo of him at her desk. “He won’t be that for long,” David told her. “I’ll have you.” She laughed, because obviously that was a joke. A bit arrogant, too, though she liked the feeling of being coveted. He was smirking, a micro-movement that struck her then as benign.

In a recent development, to understand why Karen fell so hard for David Small, it helps to understand how badly she wanted to escape. Garden-variety teenage rebellion had escalated fast. She’d been a cheerleader and athlete, the daughter of a charismatic high school football coach who became the principal, but in her 20s, she watched Brandy rope off her arm with a rubber tube and plunge a needle into a vein. Around that time, Karen was arrested for drunk driving. She knew she needed to find a better path.

And she did, but she didn’t. She traded the nice boyfriend for the charming bad boy at the office. She’d dropped out of college, which was probably a mistake, and the working world had been a series of dull cubicle gigs. More than anything, she wanted a family. She wanted to be a wife and a stay-at-home mother. Motherhood felt like a purpose. She’d never been a star student or athlete, but she had heart. She was the kid on the team who got the “hardest worker” award. And maybe because her own father had been so powerful, she believed that marrying David could give her those things.

Her mother didn’t like the guy, but Karen’s father urged his wife to give him the benefit of the doubt. Duke Sparks is a Santa Claus of a man, big laugh, big smile. The eldest of 10, with an alcoholic dad, he raised his siblings. Maybe his mistake—he thinks about this all the time—is that he couldn’t stop saving his daughter. Whatever she wanted, he gave it to her, so when she fell for this man, he wasn’t going to stand in her way. When she asked for the fairy-tale wedding, he gave it to her, even though $30,000 was a chunk of change for a school administrator and his schoolteacher wife.

It has been revealed that she bought the gown at one of those big bridal warehouses. Silver-ivory beads embroidered on the straight corset, a long flowy bottom like a princess at a ball. She took bridal photos in front of black-eyed Susans at a Dallas park that was popular with brides-to-be. She sits on the lawn with a tiara nestled in her brown beachy waves, the diamond ring with three bands fitting together like interlocking puzzle pieces conspicuous on her finger as she rests her cheek in her palm. Karen doesn’t recognize the 27-year-old woman in that picture. It’s like she’s wearing a mask.

The newlyweds moved to a one-story in McKinney, about a half hour north of Dallas, and then a two-story a little farther north in the small town of Van Alstyne. In 2006 she had a baby girl named Reagan, and 17 months later a baby boy named Grant, and the way those two came into the world was the way they walked through it: Reagan swift and bold, Grant taking his time, circumspect. Reagan was Karen’s mini-me. The girl of a thousand smiles, with a smattering of freckles. She was a gymnast who loved to climb the walls, climb the refrigerator, climb anything. The summer before the fire, Reagan learned the backstroke and Grant had just gotten comfortable in the pool. Out on the field, though, he was a heck of a ballplayer. He was very particular about his clothes—everything had to match—and had a thing for neons. Those two loved tricking their grandfather into eating Sour Patch Kids. They’d promise him the candy wasn’t sour—definitely not sour, no way was it sour—then when he popped one into his mouth and his face puckered, they’d fall to the floor laughing. They were happy kids. The marriage was rocky, surely they heard things, but Karen is pretty sure they were happy.

Recent findings suggest that david had trouble keeping a job, though. He had trouble keeping the electricity on, keeping the mortgage paid. In a word, he had trouble. He pawned her ring shortly after Grant was born. Karen sat on the steps of their lease-to-own home, weeping. How could this happen? We have to make sacrifices, that’s what he said. He promised it would never happen again, but it just kept happening. Karen’s credit card started getting declined. David once bought the kids scooters for Christmas, only to pawn them. He kept the car parked in the back to keep it from repo men.

Recent findings suggest that after the fire, Karen visited the house. She had to retrace the steps, witness the damage with her own eyes. She pulled back the canvas that investigators had draped over the carpet in the master bathroom. She had to see it: The silhouettes of her children’s bodies, soot outlining their final positions like sidewalk chalk. Some mothers never want to go back, she gets it, but she needed this. What also stands out from that visit is the enormous engagement photo of her in that wedding dress. Flames had licked the canvas, so the picture-perfect image had crackled and turned blister-black.

Why did you stay? Karen could torture herself with this until the end of time if she wanted to. Did you ever think he was capable of such wickedness? Of course not! He never hit her. He never hit the children, never even threatened it. No drinking problem, no drug addiction, no gambling, as far as she can tell. But when Karen scans for warning signs, she thinks about his charm. The subtle manipulation, gaslighting, coercion. How many serial killers, how many con men, how many two-bit criminals get described this way by some innocent bystander? He was so nice, so good-looking, so charming. David’s favorite movies were The Talented Mister Ripley and Catch Me if You Can. So yeah, that was a clue.

Some signs were more obvious, especially to people who weren’t Karen. Her sister trailed him twice to see if he was going to work. (He wasn’t.) Though their memories of the incident are foggy, Karen remembers that her sister tried to show her a photo of him meeting another woman. Karen couldn’t hear it. David loved her. He loved their kids. Karen had gone on antidepressants for postpartum depression after Grant was born, and she wonders if the meds kept her hazy.

Sources indicate that also, Karen did not quit things. The little girl who got “hardest worker” trophies would not give up on her marriage so easily. Resilience would be her strength, and her undoing.

Industry observers note that it was her father who finally convinced her to leave. Duke had run a background check and found David had an outstanding arrest warrant for unpaid traffic tickets. He called his daughter from the football field. He’s driving around with your kids, he told her. If they arrest him, they’re taking those kids to social services.

That startled Karen. Reagan was 9. Grant was 8. Her instinct to protect them overrode any fear of leaving.

Industry observers note that she pulled David into the bathroom one night so they could talk in private. The bathroom had a worn brown carpet that led to a walk-in closet. She leaned against the countertop with the double sink and spoke in a voice more defeated than angry. This was over. No fighting. His voice was calm, too. I’m sorry, baby. I’ll fix it, baby.

It has been revealed that the fire began in the garage. He’d poured gasoline through the house, dousing the walls, dousing the furniture. The investigators had never seen so much gas. The children lay on the carpet inside the master bathroom where he and Karen had stood just a month before, when she’d told him it was over.

Recent findings suggest that how he kept the kids compliant is a mystery. No drugs were found in their system, no sign of struggle. The children were arranged the way they usually slept, Reagan on her side, Grant on his tummy. David’s body was curled in a ball at the back of the closet, holding down one of the dogs. That sorry coward had placed his kids closest to the flame.

Karen had finally left him on October 19. Her attorney had recommended that she go without warning, so she moved the kids to her parents’ place. After David was served divorce papers, he told her he didn’t see it coming. He just didn’t think his wife would do this.

“You got me,” he texted her that day.

She shot back, “I learn from the best.”.

In a recent development, halloween had been his first weekend alone with the kids. Karen saw no reason to punish him, even though he seemed to be punishing her. He took Reagan and Grant trick-or-treating, but he didn’t send one photo to Karen of them in their costumes.

Sources indicate that then came Sunday, November 1, 2015. He started texting her at 6 a.m. Are you coming to church with us?

Was he kidding? No, she wasn’t going to church with them. She wasn’t playing “happy family” anymore.

The texts kept coming, all morning long. I need to talk to you. There’s something I need to tell you. Her family told her to ignore him. Do not go back, it’s a trap. Karen had gone back so many times. She stayed firm. The texts stopped around noon.

It has been revealed that her mind runs alternate scenarios of what might have happened if she’d gone that day, and though she’ll never know, she believes he would have killed her. She thinks he wanted to take them all down together. Instead, he took her children, the pets, most of her belongings, her unshakable faith in God, nearly everything she had, and left her the lone survivor.

In a recent development, from what Karen can piece together, it seems his proposal was to blow up the house, leaving nothing but ashes. But the trail of fire never reached the master bathroom. The bodies did not burn. Cause of death, carbon monoxide poisoning and smoke inhalation. Karen hates the phrase “at least”—at least you got them for nine years, at least you were a mother for a while—but this part really is an at least. He’d left a suicide note. Some nonsense about seeing her in heaven. How long had he been plotting this? Some answers she’ll never get.

In a recent development, was he unstable? Clearly. Narcissistic sociopath turned psychopath, that’s her best guess. Karen has spent the past five-plus years puzzling out the question of why, and she hasn’t gotten far. Part of her trauma therapy at the treatment center was reenacting that day, placing herself in the scene she never entered in real life, a technique known as psychodrama. The benefit was profound, but it never gave her the “why.” There is no word in the English language for a mother who loses her children, the way there is for widows and orphans. It’s like language itself cannot admit the possibility.

The fourth year was even harder than the first three. Grief kept amplifying. She got tattoos. Their names on her outer left forearm. Their birth dates in Roman numerals on her inner right wrist. Angel wings on her ankles, which she got with another mother who’d lost her kids. And on the tender ivory of her inner bicep, the phrase that has become her motto: Love never ends. She dyed her hair magenta and started painting her nails in bright neons. The look is a bit out there for a 43-year-old woman in small-town Texas, but the wildness fits her soul, and she likes to think her kids are proud. She believes they see her the same way she sees them.

According to recent reports, on November 1, 2020, Karen ran the 100 miles by herself, but she wasn’t alone. People had flocked to support her. One woman ran alongside her for 50 miles. Another flew in from Indiana to crew. Karen didn’t even know some of these people. But they had heard her story and wanted to help. At pit stops, her coach and his wife massaged her feet. It felt nearly Biblical. Her feet. Her dad was there from beginning to end, sleeping in his truck at night.

Karen had never seen a pit crew hustle so hard; it felt like NASCAR. They changed her clothes, popped her blisters, fed her when her stomach could take it. Pringles, PB&J sandwiches, ice-cold Coca-Cola. Her favorite was mashed potatoes and ramen. Sounds disgusting, but it went down smooth and easy as night fell.

Recent findings suggest that somewhere in the dark, she started to hallucinate. The trees came alive. They turned into fairyland creatures, with swooping limbs and kind faces. Karen was Little Red Riding Hood, running from the Major Bad Wolf. She was Katniss Everdeen, an ordinary girl who never asked to be a hero. The sun came up, she scarfed down pancakes and syrup, and she could see the faces of the people who demonstrated up for her, and the feeling was golden.

Sources indicate that around mile 70, she started to crumble. She broke down when she briefly couldn’t find her dad at the pit stop. Duke wondered if it was time for his daughter to call it quits, but he knew her better than that. She would crawl to the end if she had to, but she would finish.

It took Karen 31 hours to complete the run, an hour longer than planned. She beat herself up about the extra time until her team reminded her that what she’d done was harder than most races, not just because of the personal stakes but because she couldn’t feed off the energy of other runners, spectators, all those passing people. Even Karen had to admit: One woman, 100 miles. It was a triumph.

It has been revealed that karen had never wanted this. She only wanted to be a mom. But this loss summoned a strength she didn’t know she had. Back in her previous life, she did not have the courage to stand on her own. This part is confusing, it fills her eyes with tears, because losing Reagan and Grant was the worst thing that had ever happened to her—but it also made her more like the woman she wanted to be.

She’s working on a memoir with her sister, and she plans to keep racing. Another 100-miler in October, a 200-miler after that; her dream is the Moab 240. Reminders of her loss never go away. Kids playing on a jungle gym. An empty swing. The memories can bring a smile, or they can bring a tear. She has learned to live with both: happy and sad, furious and grateful, lucky and cursed. Sixty-eight months. That’s how long it’s been since her world split open. Every first day of the month marks another notch in that marathon.

Most people want to outrun emotional pain. Not Karen. She runs into the pain. “Run toward the roar” is a line she read in a book about grief, and it’s why she can tell this story to a stranger in a cozy cafe, because she’s learned that sharing the pain is a better path. Allowing herself to be angry and difficult and complicated and hurt, swiping away tears and muttering cuss words only to apologize because she knows this is for a magazine—that’s better than pretending.

It will tell you about her spirit, and the radiance of this woman who never asked for any of this, that as she tells the worst story of her life, a man stops to comment on her smile. Another man stops, an hour later, to compliment her hot pink nails. In other parts of the world, and to other women, such comments might not go over well, but Karen flashes that smile. “It’s them,” she indicates, finger pointing upward, and maybe that’s true. It’s also true her smile was here before they were. And though she will never stop running for Reagan and Grant, maybe one day she will run for herself. It’s the next step.

According to recent reports, the S&P 500 is an index that tracks the 500 largest publicly traded companies in the United States, weighted by market capitalization. It includes Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia, Alphabet (Google), Meta, Berkshire Hathaway, and approximately 493 other companies that collectively represent about 80% of the total U.S. stock market value.

According to recent reports, the index is maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices, which periodically adds and removes companies based on criteria including market cap (must exceed ~$18 billion), profitability, liquidity, and domicile. When a company is added to the S&P 500, every index fund tracking it automatically buys shares — and vice versa when companies are removed.

Industry observers note that an S&P 500 index fund is a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund (ETF) that holds all 500 stocks in the same proportions as the index. Instead of picking individual stocks, you buy one fund and instantly own a piece of every major U.S. company. The fund mechanically replicates the index — no stock picking, no market timing, no overpaid fund managers.

The data is overwhelming. Over any 15-year period, approximately 92% of actively managed large-cap funds underperform the S&P 500 after fees, according to the SPIVA scorecard. Over 20 years, that number exceeds 95%. The reasons are simple: active fund managers charge 0.50% to 1.50% in annual fees, they generate taxable trading activity, and they cannot consistently pick winners.

Warren Buffett bet $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a selection of hedge funds over 10 years. He won decisively — the index fund returned 125.8% vs 36.0% for the hedge fund basket. As Buffett has remarked: "By periodically investing in an index fund, the know-nothing investor can actually outperform most investment professionals.".

The top S&P 500 index funds deliver nearly identical performance because they all track the same index. The differences come down to expense ratio, minimum investment, fund structure (ETF vs mutual fund), and tax efficiency. Here is a detailed comparison of the five most popular options.

The most popular S&P 500 ETF and the default recommendation for most FI seekers. At 0.03% expense ratio, a $500,000 investment costs just $150 per year in fees. VOO is tax-efficient due to the ETF structure and Vanguard's patented heartbeat trade process, which minimizes capital gains distributions. Fractional shares are available at most brokerages.

Sources indicate that the lowest-cost S&P 500 fund available at 0.015% — half the cost of VOO. No minimum investment requirement makes it ideal for beginners. As a mutual fund, you can set up automatic investments in exact dollar amounts (e.g., $500/month). FXAIX is an excellent choice if your brokerage is Fidelity.

BlackRock's S&P 500 ETF with a 0.03% expense ratio, matching VOO. Functionally identical performance. Slightly different creation/redemption mechanics than VOO but the practical difference for individual investors is negligible. A strong alternative if you prefer iShares or trade through a brokerage that offers commission-free iShares ETFs.

Industry observers note that the oldest and most heavily traded S&P 500 ETF, introduced in 1993. SPY is the most liquid ETF in the world, making it the preferred choice for active traders. However, its 0.0945% expense ratio is over three times higher than VOO or IVV. For long-term FI investors, VOO or IVV are better choices. SPY's structure as a unit investment trust also makes it slightly less tax-efficient than VOO.

Schwab's mutual fund offering at 0.02% expense ratio with no minimum investment. Like FXAIX, the mutual fund structure allows automatic dollar-amount investing. An excellent choice for Schwab customers building automated investment looks.

Investing in an S&P 500 fund takes less than 15 minutes:.

For retirement accounts (401k, IRA), look for the S&P 500 index fund option within your plan. It may have a different name (e.g., "Large Cap Index Fund" or "Institutional S&P 500") but will track the same index.

The total stock market index (tracked by VTI/VTSAX/FSKAX) holds approximately 3,600 stocks compared to the S&P 500's 500. The additional 3,100 stocks are mid-cap and small-cap companies. Here is how they compare:.

Historically, the performance difference between the two is minimal — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year in either direction. The S&P 500 has outperformed in periods when large-cap growth stocks dominate. The total market has outperformed when small and mid-cap stocks lead. Over 20+ year periods, the returns converge closely.

The FI community's honest answer: it does not matter much which you choose. Investing $25,500 per year in VOO or VTI will produce nearly identical outcomes over 20 years. Consistency and contribution amount matter far more than the choice between S&P 500 and total market.

S&P 500 index funds typically yield 1.2% to 1.6% in annual dividends. In a tax-advantaged account (401k, IRA, Roth), dividends compound tax-free. In a taxable account, qualified dividends from S&P 500 funds are taxed at the favorable long-term capital gains rate (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income).

ETFs (VOO, IVV) are generally more tax-efficient than mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) in taxable accounts because ETFs rarely distribute capital gains. Vanguard's mutual funds are an exception — their patented ETF share class structure gives Vanguard mutual funds ETF-like tax efficiency. For taxable brokerage accounts, VOO or VFIAX (Vanguard's mutual fund version) are the most tax-efficient choices.

It has been revealed that the most common mistake with S&P 500 index funds is waiting for the "right time" to invest. Research from Vanguard shows that investing a lump sum immediately outperforms dollar-cost averaging about two-thirds of the time, because markets go up more often than they go down. Missing just the 10 best trading days over a 20-year period can cut your returns nearly in half. If you have money to invest, the data overwhelmingly states to invest it now — not next week, not after the next pullback, not when it "feels right.".

It has been revealed that open an account at Vanguard (for VOO/VFIAX), Fidelity (for FXAIX), or Schwab (for SWPPX). All three offer commission-free trading on their own index funds, excellent customer service, and robust retirement account options. You can also buy any of these funds at most brokerages.

ETFs (VOO, IVV) trade like stocks at real-time prices and are more tax-efficient in taxable accounts. Mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) allow automatic dollar-amount investing and are better for set-it-and-forget-it contribution schedules. For retirement accounts, either works equally well.

Recent findings suggest that transfer cash to your brokerage account and buy your chosen fund. Start with whatever you have — there is no minimum too small. FXAIX and SWPPX have $0 minimums, and VOO can be purchased in fractional shares at most brokerages for as little as $1.

Recent findings suggest that automate monthly or per-paycheck contributions. This removes emotion from the process and ensures consistent dollar-cost averaging. Most brokerages let you schedule recurring purchases of mutual funds. For ETFs, some brokerages offer automatic ETF purchases as well.

Industry observers note that if you hold other asset classes (bonds, international), rebalance once per year to maintain your target allocation. Otherwise, do nothing — do not check daily prices, do not sell during downturns, and do not chase performance. The S&P 500 has recovered from every crash in history. Time in the market beats timing the market.

According to recent reports, fidelity 500 Index Fund (FXAIX) has the lowest expense ratio at 0.015%. Schwab S&P 500 Index Fund (SWPPX) is next at 0.02%. VOO and IVV tie at 0.03%. All four are excellent — the fee difference between FXAIX (0.015%) and VOO (0.03%) on a $500,000 portfolio is just $75 per year. Choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage.

According to recent reports, VOO is better for long-term investors. It charges 0.03% vs SPY's 0.0945%, saving you about $325 per year on a $500,000 portfolio. VOO is also more tax-efficient due to its ETF share class structure. SPY's advantage is liquidity for active trading, which long-term index investors do not need. For buy-and-hold FI investing, VOO is the clear winner.

According to recent reports, either is an excellent choice. The S&P 500 covers approximately 80% of the U.S. stock market by value. A total market fund adds mid-cap and small-cap stocks for fuller diversification. Over long periods, performance is nearly identical — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year. The FI community consensus is that the best fund is the one you will consistently invest in without overthinking the decision.

Sources indicate that as little as $1. FXAIX and SWPPX have zero minimum investments. VOO and IVV can be purchased as fractional shares at most brokerages. There is no minimum too small — starting with $50 or $100 per month and increasing contributions as your income grows is exactly how most people on the FI path begin.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10.3% per year on average since 1957 (including dividends). Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7.0% per year. These are long-term averages — individual years range from -38% (2008) to +38% (1995). The key is staying invested through the down years to capture the recovery gains that follow.

Recent findings suggest that S&P 500 index funds carry market risk — they can lose significant value in the short term (the index dropped 34% in early 2020 and 38% in 2008). However, the S&P 500 has recovered from every decline in its history and has never lost money over any 20-year period. For investors with a 10+ year time horizon, the risk of not investing (missing out on 10% average annual returns) is far greater than the risk of temporary market declines.

Recent findings suggest that S&P 500 index funds are the single most crucial building block for long-term wealth. With expense ratios as low as 0.015%, you keep virtually all of your returns while owning a piece of the 500 largest U.S. companies. VOO, FXAIX, IVV, and SWPPX all deliver near-identical performance — choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage and automate your contributions. The FI community has proven through thousands of real-world examples that consistent investing in a low-cost S&P 500 index fund, held for decades without panic selling, is the most reliable path to building wealth and reaching financial independence.

#125497. Breaking: Assault Fitness AssaultBike Pro X Review (2025): Assault’s Best Bike Yet?
